# Draft:AI in Genetics, Proteomics, and Making New Medicine

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used in studies of genetics and proteomics to make medicine to treat illnesses. Genetics is the study of genes and how they are inherited to give a species a certain set of phenotypes, whereas proteomics is the study of the structure and function of proteins: the product of what genes code for.  The use of AI has implications on healthcare, bioethics, law, society, medical innovation, and research.
AlphaFold is an AI initiative produced by DeepMind that is involved in the field of proteomics; it is used to predict protein structure, which is determined by the sequence of amino acids that form the polypeptides composing said proteins. Alternative methods previously used to do this include X-ray crystallography and cryogenic electron microscopy which was slow and expensive. By using computer technology and programming, determining protein folds can be a scalable process.
Predictive models of protein shape allows for de novo protein design, which requires a determined function and the appropriate amino acids to make the protein. De novo protein design is used to reveal functions that have not been seen in nature. Proteins made from scratch can incorporate engineering concepts that allow the protein to be changeable, controlled, and incorporated into other molecular systems. Modifications can reveal similar functioning proteins with different structures to reveal slightly different properties. Controllability with a stimuli of choice makes toggling with proteins more simplistic. This controllability can be used along with other molecular systems to create desired outcomes.
Newer AI models can be created to have certain inputs give a desired output. For example, a model could make a protein with an active site when given the input of the geometry of said active site. Another possibility is to input a desired function required of a protein and the AI would create a protein to do said function. Baker Lab is an initiative by David Baker that creates protein-design software and proteins such as enzymes and transport proteins. Baker Lab created RFdiffusion, which is trained by adding Gaussian noise to a real protein structure to corrupt it and having the AI remove the noise. When it successfully does this, an input of noise without a protein is provided to the AI from which it tries to create a protein.
Background Information
Proteins get their shape from the amino acids that make up the polypeptides. All amino acids contain an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH), but each of the 20 amino acids are distinct by the remaining portion of the molecule referred to as the R group. Polypeptides, the primary structure of proteins, are made from amino acids through the dehydration synthesis of the amino group with the carboxylic acid group to form peptide bonds. The R group of the amino acids are the main components that determine the shape of the overall protein.
This general structure of an amino acid, along with an understanding of other principles of chemistry, led to the discovery of the secondary structures (i.e., α-helices and β-sheets) by Linus Pauling. While this was a major step in understanding protein structures, it was not sufficient. The methods that were used before AI included X-ray crystallography, which is when purified crystal structures of a desired substance is exposed to X-rays that form a pattern. From this pattern, the structure of the molecule is determined. A notable example of this is the discovery of the structure of myoglobin by John Kendrew in 1957 by using the blood of sperm whales; this took over a decade to resolve.
Protein Folding Problem
The protein folding problem encompasses 3 problems:
# What intramolecular forces dictate the way that polypeptides fold into proteins
# Can the folding be predicted when there is a high degree of computation
# What mechanisms are used to allow proteins to fold at different rates
What intramolecular forces dictate the way that polypeptides fold into proteins.
Here are the following ideas posed over time to resolve this problem:
* Anfinsen's Thermodynamic Hypothesis: Christian Anfinsen proposed that the shape of the protein was thermodynamically favourable, and is therefore not influenced by external molecules or enzymes. This proposition inspired protein research in laboratories as the folding would not vary from that of a biological organism.
* Dominant Force or a Combination of Forces: Although there are many molecular forces (H-bonds, Van der Waals and more) that influence structure, the hydrophobic R groups have a significant impact on the shape of the protein. Understanding of these forces are incomplete.
Can the folding be predicted when there is a high degree of computation
There have been many cases of using computational biology to resolve this question. One such example is the use of protein databases in order to predict the secondary structure of proteins. John Moult is the founder of the Critical Assessment of Techniques for Protein Structure Prediction (CASP), which has motivated development in computational methods to match predictions with known protein structures.
What mechanisms are used to allow proteins to fold at different rates
This problem points to the speed at which proteins conform to their thermodynamically favourable structure. Levinthal's Paradox (created by Cyrus Levinthal) states that finding the right conformation state by brute force would take a very long time, but proteins are capable of finding it within a short amount of time (roughly seconds). The paradox can be explain with mathematical models that suggest many conformations to be improbable. This greatly reduces the time to something reasonable.
Resolving this problem has huge implications as mentioned.
AlphaFold
AlphaFold is an AI initiative started by Demis Hassabis and lead by John Jumper. The way the AI functioned involved a particular amino acid sequence and an understanding of evolution. Similar proteins exists in various species but with slight mutations in certain regions. Understanding how the structure is preserved while still having certain mutations helps reveal how an amino acid affects the structure and the proximity of amino acids in the tertiary structure.  The proximity of 2 amino acids is then represented in a 2 x 2 matrix, which is used by a separate algorithm to determine folds. This was very successful in CASP13: getting a score of 70%. The threshold that was needed was 90% which would come in 2020.  The creation of AlphaFold has significantly increased the amount of to 200 million from roughly a hundred thousand.
Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages
* Results in rapid innovation in many parts of life such as health and environment.
* AlphaFold data is open-source and is very vast (200 million proteins in the recent version), thus allowing for easy access to information.
* Reduces tediousness and costs that are associated with comparing genome sequences and finding protein structures, thus allowing for scalability if there is enough computational power provided.
* It can be seen as ethical since the no animals were needed to determine the structure of the protein unlike X-ray Crystallography.
Disadvantages
* High degree of precision is required to enable more powerful AI prompts like synthesizing a protein from a given function. Slight deviations can result in complete failure of the protein’s ability to function.
* AI is limited to the data it has to work with and can therefore be limited in the kind of prompts it can do.  Data is acquired through genetic profiles along with traits regarding an individual's health, but many genetic diseases do not make up a significant population to be impactful for training AI or creating meaningful insights. Furthermore, diagnoses of certain genetic ailments are expensive or tedious to measure.
* When it comes to linking genetic sequences with genetic disease, AI-studies may not understand the complexity of how these links work. This is the case with non-Mendelian inheritance, where traits are not determined by dominance and recessiveness of particular alleles.
Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues
Ethical Issues
* AI relies on training data to have greater accuracy in terms of output. This data comes from sensitive genetic and health information, which raises concerns about data security and privacy, misuse of information, and consent to using data for particular research. Proposed resolutions include policies pushing for increased transparency in handling data to maintain public trust and protect individual’s genetic data.
* AI algorithms are also at risk of being programmed with bias from the training data, since false patterns can be derived from training data and could therefore give inaccurate insights that lead to disparities in the healthcare system. Keeping the AI source code transparent allows for various professionals to evaluate the fairness of the AI itself.
* The lack of transparency and understanding of how AI derives its insights can make the tool less credible in drug discovery and healthcare; this is referred to as the Black-Box Problem. Stakeholders can make a proper investment of time, labour, and money towards initiatives like this if the tools being developed are understandable to the general public.
Legal Matters
* AI policies are put in place by various nations and organizations such as USA, China, and The European Union (EU).
* Some initiative by government including aiding AI companies to navigate risks, bans on certain uses of AI and highly specific regulations on AI that poses high-risk (such as the health sector)
Social Issues
* AI can contain social biases when it is trained on user-generated data that have social biases.
* AI can have an impact on positions that humans would have taken in the health care industry. An increased dependency on AI requires transparency and accountability from bad actors.
Notable Example: Malaria Vaccine by the University of Oxford
The Pfs48/45 molecule is a potential candidate for a vaccine in malaria resistance. Its structure has been determined using AlphaFold2 and was confirmed using X-ray Crystallography. It was revealed that the desired protein had a disc like structure, which makes it ideally placed for its function in preventing the transmission of malaria.
